title: Taming the Need to Control
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines the internal conflict between a leader's desire for excellent outcomes and the trust required to empower a team to deliver them. It describes how leaders with the highest standards often become 'control freaks' and traces the self-destructive loop that follows. The prescribed fix is incremental, leaders should pre-decide specific tasks and decisions they can delegate completely, starting small and expanding the list as trust and outcomes improve. The piece frames giving up control not as a compromise but as the actual mechanism for achieving excellent outcomes.
points: High-standard leaders often become controlling precisely because they don't trust others to meet their bar, creating a self-destructive loop.
Once team members feel distrusted, they disengage from execution and become passive spectators rather than active contributors.
The prescribed fix is incremental: pre-decide specific tasks that can be fully delegated, starting small and expanding over successive projects.
Giving up control is reframed not as a compromise on excellence but as the actual mechanism that produces better outcomes.
quotes: In their desire to achieve the greatest outcome, they become dictators of control.
Overcoming the need for total control is never easy for leaders driven to excel. Most control freaks have incredibly high standards and don’t trust others to meet them, hence the need for control.
Once team members feel distrusted, they turn a blind eye toward execution. They quickly become spectators and not doers.
The key is to pre-decide what details and processes the leader can delegate completely to others. If the conclusion is none of them, they are simply not ready to escape the loop.
Giving up some control is actually the best way to create great results. Who knew? Everyone but the control freak.
